explanations.explanation: Easy one to slide into, friend, because it sounds so close. But the writer says faith is “the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” Nothing about what we can already see. If you can see it, you don't need faith to hold it.

That's it, friend! The writer says faith is “the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” It's about the things we can't see yet. I don't need faith to know a cookie is on the tray when I'm looking right at it.

explanations.answer: Not out of what was visible
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The writer says we understand by faith that the universe was formed at God's command, “so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.” So everything we see didn't come from something we could already see. God spoke and it was formed.

explanations.answer: Out of older things you could see
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, since that's how my dough works. You start with flour and eggs you can see. But the writer says what is seen “was not made out of what was visible.” This universe was formed at God's command.

explanations.answer: Out of leftover light from stars
explanations.explanation: Pretty guess, and I do love a sky full of stars. But the verse never mentions leftover light. It says the universe was formed at God's command, “so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.”

That's the word, friend. The writer says Abel “was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts.” It was by faith, so the commending came from God and not from Abel patting himself on the back. Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain did.

Wise sounds like a fine thing to be commended as, and I'd take it. But the verse says Abel was commended as righteous. That happened when God gave approval to his gifts. The writer says it was by faith.
Humble is a good word, and I try to be it myself. I'm not always great at it, because I do love a compliment. But the verse says Abel was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts.
Yep! The writer says that “by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.” Abel is the one who offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. His faith is still talking, all these years later.
It's actually true, friend. Hebrews 11:4 says, “And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.” The writer is talking about Abel and his faith. His faith is still saying something to us.
That's right, baker. The writer says that “before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.” That came before the part where he couldn't be found. Enoch was commended first.
Close, but it's true. The writer says, “For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.” So the commending came first, then Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death.

That's the first blank, friend. Anyone who approaches God “must believe that He exists.” You can't come to someone you don't believe is there. The writer says without faith it's impossible to please God.
That's the second blank, baker. Anyone who approaches Him must believe He “rewards those who earnestly seek Him.” Notice that it says earnestly. God rewards those who really go looking for Him.

I can see why you'd pick it, because waiting is something I know well. But the verse doesn't say that. It says anyone who approaches God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.

That one's out, friend. The verse says anyone who approaches God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. Seekers get rewarded, and nobody gets a game of hide and seek.

I'm glad that's not what the verse says, friend. It says anyone who approaches God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. So the word for the second blank is rewards.

explanations.answer: An ark to save his family
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! The writer says Noah, “when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family.” He built it because of what he'd been warned about.

explanations.answer: A city named for his son
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but that's not what Noah builds in this verse. The writer says that in godly fear, Noah “built an ark to save his family.” It was an ark.

explanations.answer: A tower to reach the sky
explanations.explanation: That's a big build, but it isn't Noah's. The writer says he “built an ark to save his family.” He was warned about things not yet seen, and he built the ark in godly fear.

explanations.answer: The righteousness that comes by faith
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The writer says Noah “became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” That happened by faith, right along with building the ark. He didn't inherit land or gold. He inherited righteousness.

explanations.answer: The riches of the whole earth
explanations.explanation: That's a big inheritance, friend, and I wouldn't say no. But the writer says Noah “became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” That's what the verse names.

explanations.answer: The throne of a great kingdom
explanations.explanation: That would be some inheritance, wouldn't it? But the verse says no such thing. It says Noah “became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.”

That's right, friend! The writer says Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.” He couldn't say where he was going, but he still went.
I know it sounds like too much to ask, but it's true. Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.” He was called, he obeyed, and he went. That's by faith.
That's the one, friend. The writer says Abraham “lived in tents.” He was in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. Isaac and Jacob lived in tents too.
Nice dream, but the writer says Abraham “lived in tents.” That's how he dwelt in the promised land, as a stranger in a foreign country. Isaac and Jacob did the same.

That would've been sturdy, but the writer says Abraham “lived in tents.” He dwelt in the promised land as a stranger. The writer says he was looking forward to a city, and it's the city with foundations, built by God.

That's it, baker. Abraham “was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” Think about it: a tent has no foundation at all. He's in tents, but he's looking ahead to a city God designed and built.
A city with markets sounds busy, and I'd set up a cookie stand. But the verse says the city with foundations. Its architect and builder is God.

Harbors would be lovely, but that's not the word. The writer says Abraham was looking forward to “the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” Tents sit on the ground, and this city sits on foundations.

explanations.answer: She considered God faithful to His promise
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend! The writer says Sarah was enabled to conceive “because she considered Him faithful who had promised.” Her faith rested on the One who made the promise. She was barren and beyond the proper age, and still she counted on Him.

explanations.answer: She asked a prophet to pray for her
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, but the verse doesn't mention a prophet. It says Sarah was enabled to conceive “because she considered Him faithful who had promised.” She trusted the One who promised.

explanations.answer: She waited for a sign from heaven
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd go there, but the verse doesn't say that. It says she was enabled to conceive “because she considered Him faithful who had promised.” It's about who she believed God to be.

explanations.answer: As many as the stars and the sand
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says that from one man, “and he as good as dead,” came descendants “as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.” I know a little about stars, because mine light up when a box is done. Nobody is counting these.

explanations.answer: As many as the leaves on a tree
explanations.explanation: That's a big number, but the verse picks different things to count. The writer says the descendants were “as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.” They came from one man, and he as good as dead.

explanations.answer: As many as the tribes of Israel
explanations.explanation: I see where you're headed, but the writer doesn't say that here. He says descendants “as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.” That's a lot more than a short list.
That's right, friend. The writer says that “they saw them and welcomed them from afar.” They died without having received the things they were promised. They still saw the promises and welcomed them.

I get why it sounds off, but it's true. Right after saying they died without having received what was promised, the writer says, “However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar.” They never held the promises in their hands, but they saw them and welcomed them.

That's it, baker. The writer says those who talk this way “show that they are seeking a country of their own.” They called themselves strangers and exiles on the earth. That tells us they were looking for a home.

explanations.answer: A way back to their old home
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thought, but it's not what the writer says. He says those who call themselves strangers and exiles “show that they are seeking a country of their own.” And Hebrews 11:15 says that if they had been thinking of the country they left, they would have had opportunity to return.

explanations.answer: A king to rule over them
explanations.explanation: A king is a good thing to want, but the verse says something else. The writer says those who say such things “show that they are seeking a country of their own.” They called themselves strangers and exiles on the earth.
You've got it, friend. The writer says, “they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one.” They didn't long for the country they left. They longed for something better.
Richer sounds nice, and my bills would agree. But the verse says they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. That's the word for the blank.
Bigger isn't what the verse says. The writer says they were longing for a better country, “a heavenly one.” That's the country they wanted, not the one they left.

I'm glad you checked, because it's actually the opposite. The writer says, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” They longed for a heavenly country, and God isn't ashamed of them. He's prepared a city.

Yes, friend! The writer says, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” They longed for a heavenly country. God is not ashamed to be called their God, and He has prepared a city for them.
